lesson.title: Is-A: Testing Whether Inheritance Actually Makes Sense
lesson.summary: The is-a relationship is the logical test behind inheritance: a child class should only inherit from a parent class when every instance of the child genuinely qualifies as an instance of the parent too.
lesson.body:
In the has-a section, you saw that composition models ownership: a Car has an Engine. Inheritance models something different and stronger: identity. When Bird inherits from Animal, you are claiming that a Bird is-a Animal, not merely that it uses one. That distinction is the single most useful design question in object-oriented programming, and it is worth pausing on before writing any more inheritance hierarchies.

Python gives you two built-in tools to check and enforce is-a relationships. `isinstance(object, Class)` asks whether a specific object counts as that class, or any of its parent classes. `issubclass(ClassA, ClassB)` asks the same question one level up, about the classes themselves rather than a specific object.

```python
class Animal:
    pass

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

d = Dog()
print(isinstance(d, Animal))
print(isinstance(d, Dog))
print(issubclass(Dog, Animal))
print(issubclass(Animal, Dog))
```

This prints `True`, `True`, `True`, and finally `False`. A Dog object is an instance of both Dog and Animal, because Dog inherited from Animal, and inheritance is transitive up the chain. But the relationship only runs one direction: Dog is a subclass of Animal, so `issubclass(Dog, Animal)` is `True`, while `issubclass(Animal, Dog)` is `False`, since not every Animal is specifically a Dog.

This is-a test is what should decide whether you reach for inheritance at all. A Dog is-a Animal, so inheritance is a sensible fit. But a Car is not an Engine, it merely has one, which is exactly why the earlier example used composition instead of inheritance for that relationship. A useful sanity check, sometimes called the Liskov substitution idea, is this: if you cannot honestly finish the sentence "a Child is a Parent, in every situation the Parent is used," then the classes should probably use has-a composition instead of is-a inheritance. Getting this choice right up front is what keeps class hierarchies sensible as a codebase grows, rather than turning into a tangle of classes that technically compile but do not model reality.
